Appendix A Proof of the Unfolding Theorem

A.1 Setup and notation

Let Ωn⊂ℝ3​n\Omega^{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3n} be the fundamental domain (simulation cell for all nn electrons). The lattice of composite translations ℒn={𝐓𝐌:𝐌∈ℤ3​n}\mathcal{L}^{n}=\{\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}}:\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3n}\} tiles ℝ3​n\mathbb{R}^{3n} exactly, i.e. ℝ3​n=⨆𝐌∈ℤ3​n(Ωn+𝐓𝐌)\mathbb{R}^{3n}=\bigsqcup_{\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3n}}(\Omega^{n}+\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}}). The periodized basis functions are Φk​(𝐫)=∑𝐌ϕk​(𝐫−𝐓𝐌)\Phi_{k}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\mathbf{M}}\phi_{k}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}}).

A.2 Proof of Theorem 1

The matrix element of O^\hat{O} in the periodized basis is, by definition,

Ok​l=∫ΩnΦk∗​(𝐫)​O^​Φl​(𝐫)​𝑑𝐫.O_{kl}=\int_{\Omega^{n}}\Phi_{k}^{*}(\mathbf{r})\,\hat{O}\,\Phi_{l}(\mathbf{r})\,d\mathbf{r}. (95)

Expanding both sums:

Ok​l=∑𝐌k,𝐌l∈ℤ3​n∫Ωnϕk∗​(𝐫−𝐓𝐌k)​O^​ϕl​(𝐫−𝐓𝐌l)​𝑑𝐫.O_{kl}=\sum_{\mathbf{M}_{k},\mathbf{M}_{l}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3n}}\int_{\Omega^{n}}\phi_{k}^{*}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{k}})\,\hat{O}\,\phi_{l}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{l}})\,d\mathbf{r}. (96)
Step 1: Shift the integration variable.

For each fixed 𝐌k\mathbf{M}_{k}, apply the change of variables 𝐫↦𝐫+𝐓𝐌k\mathbf{r}\mapsto\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{k}}:

Ok​l=∑𝐌k,𝐌l∫Ωn+𝐓𝐌kϕk∗​(𝐫)​[O^​ϕl]​(𝐫−𝐓𝐌l−𝐌k)​𝑑𝐫.O_{kl}=\sum_{\mathbf{M}_{k},\mathbf{M}_{l}}\int_{\Omega^{n}+\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{k}}}\phi_{k}^{*}(\mathbf{r})\,\bigl[\hat{O}\,\phi_{l}\bigr](\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{l}-\mathbf{M}_{k}})\,d\mathbf{r}. (97)

Here we used the lattice-periodicity condition Eq. (33): the kernel of O^\hat{O} satisfies K⁡(𝐫+𝐓𝐌k,𝐫′+𝐓𝐌k)=K⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)K(\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{k}},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}+\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{k}})=K(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}), so acting with O^\hat{O} and then shifting is the same as first shifting the argument of ϕl\phi_{l}. Concretely, for any function ff:

[O^f(⋅−𝐓𝐌l)](𝐫+𝐓𝐌k)=[O^f(⋅−𝐓𝐌l−𝐌k)](𝐫).\bigl[\hat{O}\,f(\cdot-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{l}})\bigr](\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{k}})=\bigl[\hat{O}\,f(\cdot-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{l}-\mathbf{M}_{k}})\bigr](\mathbf{r}). (98)
Step 2: Promote the cell integral to all space.

Since {Ωn+𝐓𝐌k}𝐌k∈ℤ3​n\{\Omega^{n}+\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{k}}\}_{\mathbf{M}_{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3n}} is a disjoint partition of ℝ3​n\mathbb{R}^{3n}, summing over 𝐌k\mathbf{M}_{k} converts the integral over each translated cell into a single integral over all of ℝ3​n\mathbb{R}^{3n}:

Ok​l=∑𝐌l−𝐌k=:𝐌(∑𝐌k1)∫ℝ3​nϕk∗(𝐫)O^ϕl(𝐫−𝐓𝐌)d𝐫.O_{kl}=\sum_{\mathbf{M}_{l}-\mathbf{M}_{k}=:\mathbf{M}}\left(\sum_{\mathbf{M}_{k}}1\right)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3n}}\phi_{k}^{*}(\mathbf{r})\,\hat{O}\,\phi_{l}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}})\,d\mathbf{r}. (99)

The inner sum ∑𝐌k\sum_{\mathbf{M}_{k}} is simply the number of times a fixed difference 𝐌=𝐌l−𝐌k\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{M}_{l}-\mathbf{M}_{k} is realized, which is exactly once for each 𝐌∈ℤ3​n\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3n}. This yields Eq. (34). □\square

Remark on convergence.

The interchange of sum and integral is justified whenever ϕk​(𝐫)​(O^​ϕl)​(𝐫−𝐓𝐌)\phi_{k}(\mathbf{r})\,(\hat{O}\phi_{l})(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}}) is absolutely summable over 𝐌\mathbf{M} in L1​(ℝ3​n)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3n}). For Gaussian basis functions, the integrand decays as e−𝐝𝐌T​C~k​l​𝐝𝐌e^{-\mathbf{d}_{\mathbf{M}}^{T}\widetilde{C}_{kl}\mathbf{d}_{\mathbf{M}}} (exponentially in |𝐌|2|\mathbf{M}|^{2}), so this is always satisfied.

A.3 Proof of Theorem 2 (Bloch generalization)

The Bloch matrix element is

Ok​l(𝐤B)=∑𝐌k,𝐌le−i𝐤B⋅𝐓𝐌ke+i𝐤B⋅𝐓𝐌l∫Ωnϕk∗(𝐫−𝐓𝐌k)O^ϕl(𝐫−𝐓𝐌l)d𝐫.O_{kl}^{(\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{B}})}=\sum_{\mathbf{M}_{k},\mathbf{M}_{l}}e^{-i\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{B}}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{k}}}e^{+i\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{B}}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{l}}}\int_{\Omega^{n}}\phi_{k}^{*}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{k}})\,\hat{O}\,\phi_{l}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{l}})\,d\mathbf{r}. (100)

Applying Steps 1–2 of the Theorem 1 proof, the 𝐌k\mathbf{M}_{k}-sum again promotes the integral to ℝ3​n\mathbb{R}^{3n}, leaving the phase ei​𝐤B⋅(𝐓𝐌l−𝐓𝐌k)=ei​𝐤B⋅𝐓𝐌e^{i\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{B}}\cdot(\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{l}}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}_{k}})}=e^{i\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{B}}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}}} (with 𝐌=𝐌l−𝐌k\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{M}_{l}-\mathbf{M}_{k}) attached to each term, giving Eq. (39). □\square

Table 4 summarizes how the unfolded integrand ℐ𝐌≡∫ℝ3​nϕkO^ϕl(⋅−𝐓𝐌)d𝐫\mathcal{I}_{\mathbf{M}}\equiv\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3n}}\phi_{k}\,\hat{O}\,\phi_{l}(\cdot-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}})\,d\mathbf{r} depends on the operator class.

=\displaystyle= erf⁡(R/σ)R,\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{erf}(R/\sigma)}{R},

𝒥𝐌(i​j)=ω𝐌​𝒮k​l​erf⁡(|u¯i​j,𝐌|/σi​j,s)|u¯i​j,𝐌|,\mathcal{J}_{\mathbf{M}}^{(ij)}=\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\,\mathcal{S}_{kl}\,\frac{\mathrm{erf}(|\bar{u}_{ij,\mathbf{M}}|/\sigma_{ij,s})}{|\bar{u}_{ij,\mathbf{M}}|}, (119)

with F0​(x)=π2​erf​(x)/xF_{0}(x)=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\mathrm{erf}(\sqrt{x})/\sqrt{x} giving the equivalent compact form 𝒥=(2/σi​j,s)​ω𝐌​𝒮k​l​F0​(R2/σ2)\mathcal{J}=(2/\sigma_{ij,s})\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\mathcal{S}_{kl}F_{0}(R^{2}/\sigma^{2}).

The finite limit limR→0erf⁡(R/σ)/R=2/(σ​π)\lim_{R\to 0}\mathrm{erf}(R/\sigma)/R=2/(\sigma\sqrt{\pi}) confirms regularity at zero pair separation. The electron–nuclear case follows identically with σi​j,s→σi\sigma_{ij,s}\to\sigma_{i}, |u¯i​j,𝐌|→|𝐫¯𝐌,i−𝐑I||\bar{u}_{ij,\mathbf{M}}|\to|\bar{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{M},i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|, giving Eqs. (59)–(60).

F.3 Connection to the Ewald real-space formula

Setting κ=0\kappa=0 and 𝐧=𝟎\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{0} in Eq. (49) gives erfc⁡(0)/R=1/R\mathrm{erfc}(0)/R=1/R, recovering the full [0,∞)[0,\infty) integral above. For a neutral cell all 𝐧≠𝟎\mathbf{n}\neq\mathbf{0} shells and the entire reciprocal-space sum vanish as κ→0\kappa\to 0, so the Ewald formula reduces exactly to Eqs. (59)–(60), confirming consistency.

Appendix G Delta-Function Matrix Elements and the Coulomb Potential

G.1 Overview

The contact operators δ(3)​(𝐫i−𝐫j)\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}) and δ(3)​(𝐫i−𝐒)\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{S}) have closed-form matrix elements in the SCG basis. More importantly, the Coulomb operator 1/|𝐫i−𝐫j|1/|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}| can be expressed as a weighted integral of δ(3)​(𝐫i−𝐫j−𝐮)\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}-\mathbf{u}) over 𝐮\mathbf{u}, providing a third independent derivation of the neutral Coulomb result and establishing exact equivalence with Appendix F.

G.2 Matrix element of δ(3)​(𝐫i−𝐫j)\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})

After unfolding (Theorem 1, Corollary 1a), the per-image integral is

𝒟𝐌(i​j)=∫ℝ3​nϕk​(𝐫)​δ(3)​(𝐫i−𝐫j)​ϕl​(𝐫−𝐓𝐌)​𝑑𝐫.\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{M}}^{(ij)}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3n}}\phi_{k}(\mathbf{r})\,\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})\,\phi_{l}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}})\,d\mathbf{r}. (120)

Using the combined Gaussian product and the Fourier representation δ(3)​(𝐮)=(2​π)−3​∫ei​𝐪⋅𝐮​d3​𝐪\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{u})=(2\pi)^{-3}\int e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{u}}d^{3}\mathbf{q} with 𝐮=𝐏i​jT​𝐫\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{P}_{ij}^{T}\mathbf{r}:

𝒟𝐌(i​j)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{M}}^{(ij)} =ω𝐌​∫d3​𝐪(2​π)3​ei​𝐪⋅u¯i​j,𝐌​∫ℝ3​ne−(𝐫−𝐫¯𝐌)T​A~k​l​(𝐫−𝐫¯𝐌)+i​𝐪⋅𝐏i​jT​(𝐫−𝐫¯𝐌)​𝑑𝐫.\displaystyle=\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\int\!\frac{d^{3}\mathbf{q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\bar{u}_{ij,\mathbf{M}}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3n}}e^{-(\mathbf{r}-\bar{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{M}})^{T}\widetilde{A}_{kl}(\mathbf{r}-\bar{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{M}})+i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{P}_{ij}^{T}(\mathbf{r}-\bar{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{M}})}d\mathbf{r}. (121)

The inner Gaussian integral with linear phase i​(𝐏i​j​𝐪)T​(𝐫−𝐫¯𝐌)i(\mathbf{P}_{ij}\mathbf{q})^{T}(\mathbf{r}-\bar{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{M}}) gives 𝒮k​lexp(−𝐪T𝐏i​jTA~k​l−1𝐏i​j𝐪/4)=𝒮k​le−σi​j,s2|𝐪|2/4\mathcal{S}_{kl}\exp(-\mathbf{q}^{T}\mathbf{P}_{ij}^{T}\widetilde{A}_{kl}^{-1}\mathbf{P}_{ij}\mathbf{q}/4)=\mathcal{S}_{kl}e^{-\sigma_{ij,s}^{2}|\mathbf{q}|^{2}/4}. The remaining 𝐪\mathbf{q}-integral is an inverse Fourier transform of a Gaussian:

𝒟𝐌(i​j)=ω𝐌​𝒮k​l​1(π​σi​j,s2)3/2​exp⁡(−|u¯i​j,𝐌|2σi​j,s2).\boxed{\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{M}}^{(ij)}=\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\,\mathcal{S}_{kl}\,\frac{1}{(\pi\sigma_{ij,s}^{2})^{3/2}}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{|\bar{u}_{ij,\mathbf{M}}|^{2}}{\sigma_{ij,s}^{2}}\right).} (122)

The full matrix element is

⟨Φk|δ(3)(𝐫i−𝐫j)|Φl⟩=𝒮k​l(π​σi​j,s2)3/2∑𝐌ω𝐌e−|u¯i​j,𝐌|2/σi​j,s2.\langle\Phi_{k}|\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})|\Phi_{l}\rangle=\frac{\mathcal{S}_{kl}}{(\pi\sigma_{ij,s}^{2})^{3/2}}\sum_{\mathbf{M}}\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\,e^{-|\bar{u}_{ij,\mathbf{M}}|^{2}/\sigma_{ij,s}^{2}}. (123)

The result is the combined Gaussian weight ω𝐌​𝒮k​l\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\mathcal{S}_{kl} times a three-dimensional Gaussian in the mean pair displacement u¯i​j,𝐌\bar{u}_{ij,\mathbf{M}} with width σi​j,s/2\sigma_{ij,s}/\sqrt{2}.

G.3 Matrix element of δ(3)​(𝐫i−𝐒)\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{S})

For the operator δ(3)​(𝐫i−𝐒)\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{S}) with a fixed vector 𝐒∈ℝ3\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, the projector is 𝐏i=𝐞i⊗I3\mathbf{P}_{i}=\mathbf{e}_{i}\otimes I_{3}, 𝐏iT​A~k​l−1​𝐏i=σi2​I3\mathbf{P}_{i}^{T}\widetilde{A}_{kl}^{-1}\mathbf{P}_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}I_{3}, and the mean is 𝐫¯𝐌,i\bar{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{M},i}. The identical Fourier argument gives

𝒟𝐌(i,𝐒)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{M}}^{(i,\mathbf{S})} ≡\displaystyle\equiv ∫ℝ3​nϕk​(𝐫)​δ(3)​(𝐫i−𝐒)​ϕl​(𝐫−𝐓𝐌)​𝑑𝐫\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3n}}\phi_{k}(\mathbf{r})\,\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{S})\,\phi_{l}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{M}})\,d\mathbf{r} (124)
=\displaystyle= ω𝐌​𝒮k​l​e−|𝐫¯𝐌,i−𝐒|2/σi2(π​σi2)3/2,\displaystyle\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\,\mathcal{S}_{kl}\,\frac{e^{-|\bar{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{M},i}-\mathbf{S}|^{2}/\sigma_{i}^{2}}}{(\pi\sigma_{i}^{2})^{3/2}},

and

⟨Φk|δ(3)(𝐫i−𝐒)|Φl⟩=𝒮k​l(π​σi2)3/2∑𝐌ω𝐌e−|𝐫¯𝐌,i−𝐒|2/σi2.\langle\Phi_{k}|\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{S})|\Phi_{l}\rangle=\frac{\mathcal{S}_{kl}}{(\pi\sigma_{i}^{2})^{3/2}}\sum_{\mathbf{M}}\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\,e^{-|\bar{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{M},i}-\mathbf{S}|^{2}/\sigma_{i}^{2}}. (125)

This is a Gaussian in 𝐒\mathbf{S} centred at 𝐫¯𝐌,i\bar{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{M},i}, reflecting the probability density for finding electron ii at position 𝐒\mathbf{S} in the combined Gaussian state.

The 1/r1/r operator admits the resolution

1|𝐫i−𝐫j|=∫ℝ3δ(3)​(𝐫i−𝐫j−𝐮)|𝐮|​d3​𝐮.\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}|}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}-\mathbf{u})}{|\mathbf{u}|}\,d^{3}\mathbf{u}. (126)

𝒥𝐌(i​j)=∫ℝ3𝒟𝐌(i​j,𝐮)|𝐮|​d3​𝐮,\mathcal{J}_{\mathbf{M}}^{(ij)}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{M}}^{(ij,\mathbf{u})}}{|\mathbf{u}|}\,d^{3}\mathbf{u}, (127)

𝒟𝐌(i​j,𝐮)=ω𝐌​𝒮k​l(π​σi​j,s2)3/2​exp⁡(−|u¯i​j,𝐌−𝐮|2σi​j,s2).\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{M}}^{(ij,\mathbf{u})}=\frac{\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\,\mathcal{S}_{kl}}{(\pi\sigma_{ij,s}^{2})^{3/2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{|\bar{u}_{ij,\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{u}|^{2}}{\sigma_{ij,s}^{2}}\right). (128)

Hence

𝒥𝐌(i​j)=ω𝐌​𝒮k​l(π​σi​j,s2)3/2​∫ℝ3e−|u¯i​j,𝐌−𝐮|2/σi​j,s2|𝐮|​d3​𝐮.\mathcal{J}_{\mathbf{M}}^{(ij)}=\frac{\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\,\mathcal{S}_{kl}}{(\pi\sigma_{ij,s}^{2})^{3/2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{e^{-|\bar{u}_{ij,\mathbf{M}}-\mathbf{u}|^{2}/\sigma_{ij,s}^{2}}}{|\mathbf{u}|}\,d^{3}\mathbf{u}. (129)

The remaining integral is of the standard form ∫ℝ3e−|𝐜−𝐮|2/a2/|𝐮|d3𝐮\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}e^{-|\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{u}|^{2}/a^{2}}/|\mathbf{u}|\,d^{3}\mathbf{u} with 𝐜=u¯i​j,𝐌\mathbf{c}=\bar{u}_{ij,\mathbf{M}} and a=σi​j,sa=\sigma_{ij,s}. Substituting 𝐮=a​𝐭\mathbf{u}=a\mathbf{t} and using the standard result

∫ℝ3e−|𝐭−𝐑|2|𝐭|​d3​𝐭=π3/2​erf​(|𝐑|)|𝐑|,\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{e^{-|\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{R}|^{2}}}{|\mathbf{t}|}\,d^{3}\mathbf{t}=\frac{\pi^{3/2}\,\mathrm{erf}(|\mathbf{R}|)}{|\mathbf{R}|}, (130)

with 𝐑=𝐜/a=u¯i​j,𝐌/σi​j,s\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{c}/a=\bar{u}_{ij,\mathbf{M}}/\sigma_{ij,s}:

∫ℝ3e−|𝐜−𝐮|2/a2|𝐮|​d3​𝐮\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{e^{-|\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{u}|^{2}/a^{2}}}{|\mathbf{u}|}\,d^{3}\mathbf{u} (131)
=\displaystyle= a3⋅1a∫e−|𝐭−𝐑|2|𝐭|d3𝐭\displaystyle a^{3}\cdot\frac{1}{a}\int\frac{e^{-|\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{R}|^{2}}}{|\mathbf{t}|}\,d^{3}\mathbf{t}
=\displaystyle= a2​π3/2​erf​(|𝐜|/a)|𝐜|/a\displaystyle\frac{a^{2}\pi^{3/2}\,\mathrm{erf}(|\mathbf{c}|/a)}{|\mathbf{c}|/a}
=\displaystyle= π3/2​σi​j,s3​erf​(R/σi​j,s)R,\displaystyle\frac{\pi^{3/2}\sigma_{ij,s}^{3}\,\mathrm{erf}(R/\sigma_{ij,s})}{R}, (132)

where R=|u¯i​j,𝐌|R=|\bar{u}_{ij,\mathbf{M}}|. Substituting into Eq. (129):

𝒥𝐌(i​j)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\mathbf{M}}^{(ij)} =\displaystyle= ω𝐌​𝒮k​l(π​σi​j,s2)3/2⋅π3/2​σi​j,s3​erf​(R/σi​j,s)R\displaystyle\frac{\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\,\mathcal{S}_{kl}}{(\pi\sigma_{ij,s}^{2})^{3/2}}\cdot\frac{\pi^{3/2}\sigma_{ij,s}^{3}\,\mathrm{erf}(R/\sigma_{ij,s})}{R} (133)
=\displaystyle= ω𝐌​𝒮k​l​erf⁡(R/σi​j,s)R.\displaystyle\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\,\mathcal{S}_{kl}\,\frac{\mathrm{erf}(R/\sigma_{ij,s})}{R}.

Proof of the key convolution identity (130).

Write 1/|𝐭|=(2/π)​∫0∞e−λ2​|𝐭|2​𝑑λ1/|\mathbf{t}|=(2/\sqrt{\pi})\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda^{2}|\mathbf{t}|^{2}}d\lambda and evaluate the Gaussian integral over 𝐭\mathbf{t}: ∫e−|𝐭−𝐑|2−λ2​|𝐭|2d3𝐭=[π/(1+λ2)]3/2e−λ2|𝐑|2/(1+λ2)\int e^{-|\mathbf{t}-\mathbf{R}|^{2}-\lambda^{2}|\mathbf{t}|^{2}}d^{3}\mathbf{t}=[\pi/(1+\lambda^{2})]^{3/2}e^{-\lambda^{2}|\mathbf{R}|^{2}/(1+\lambda^{2})}. Then 2π∫0∞[π/(1+λ2)]3/2e−λ2R2/(1+λ2)dλ=π3/2erf(R)/R\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}[\pi/(1+\lambda^{2})]^{3/2}e^{-\lambda^{2}R^{2}/(1+\lambda^{2})}d\lambda=\pi^{3/2}\mathrm{erf}(R)/R by the same substitution s=λ/1+λ2s=\lambda/\sqrt{1+\lambda^{2}} used in Appendix F. □\square

The electron–nuclear potential 1/|𝐫i−𝐑I|1/|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}| can similarly be written as

1|𝐫i−𝐑I|=∫ℝ3δ(3)​(𝐫i−𝐒)|𝐒−𝐑I|​d3​𝐒.\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{S})}{|\mathbf{S}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|}\,d^{3}\mathbf{S}. (134)

Using Eq. (124):

𝒥𝐌(i,I)=ω𝐌​𝒮k​l(π​σi2)3/2​∫ℝ3e−|𝐫¯𝐌,i−𝐒|2/σi2|𝐒−𝐑I|​d3​𝐒.\mathcal{J}_{\mathbf{M}}^{(i,I)}=\frac{\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\,\mathcal{S}_{kl}}{(\pi\sigma_{i}^{2})^{3/2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{e^{-|\bar{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{M},i}-\mathbf{S}|^{2}/\sigma_{i}^{2}}}{|\mathbf{S}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|}\,d^{3}\mathbf{S}. (135)

𝒥𝐌(i,I)=ω𝐌​𝒮k​l​erf⁡(|𝐫¯𝐌,i−𝐑I|/σi)|𝐫¯𝐌,i−𝐑I|,\mathcal{J}_{\mathbf{M}}^{(i,I)}=\omega_{\mathbf{M}}\,\mathcal{S}_{kl}\,\frac{\mathrm{erf}(|\bar{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{M},i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|/\sigma_{i})}{|\bar{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathbf{M},i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|}, (136)

recovering Eq. (60) upon multiplication by −ZI-Z_{I} and summation over ii, II, 𝐌\mathbf{M}. □\square

G.7 Structural interpretation

Equations (122) and (124) reveal the following structure. The SCG basis smears each electron-pair contact over a 3D Gaussian of width σi​j,s/2\sigma_{ij,s}/\sqrt{2}. The Coulomb matrix element is the convolution of this smeared contact density with the bare 1/r1/r kernel, giving the screened potential erf⁡(R/σ)/R\mathrm{erf}(R/\sigma)/R. The effective range σi​j,s=(Ak​l−1)i​i+(Ak​l−1)j​j−2​(Ak​l−1)i​j\sigma_{ij,s}=\sqrt{(A_{kl}^{-1})_{ii}+(A_{kl}^{-1})_{jj}-2(A_{kl}^{-1})_{ij}} is the standard deviation of the pair coordinate 𝐫i−𝐫j\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j} in the combined Gaussian; a more correlated basis (larger off-diagonal AkA_{k}) produces a narrower smearing and a Coulomb matrix element closer to the bare 1/r1/r result.

∂Sk​l∂(𝐬k)α\displaystyle\frac{\partial S_{kl}}{\partial(\mathbf{s}_{k})_{\alpha}} =−2𝒮k​l∑𝐌ω𝐌(C~k​l𝐝𝐌)α,\displaystyle=-2\,\mathcal{S}_{kl}\sum_{\mathbf{M}}\omega_{\mathbf{M}}(\widetilde{C}_{kl}\mathbf{d}_{\mathbf{M}})_{\alpha}, (145)

Appendix J Convergence Acceleration: Theta-Function Dual

J.1 The problem: slow convergence for diffuse basis functions

Every matrix element derived in the paper reduces, after unfolding (Theorem 1), to a lattice sum of the form

ℐ=∑M∈ℤ3​nωM​f​(dM),ωM=e−dM⊤​C~k​l​dM,dM=sk−sl−TM,\mathcal{I}=\sum_{M\in\mathbb{Z}^{3n}}\omega_{M}\,f(d_{M}),\qquad\omega_{M}=e^{-d_{M}^{\top}\tilde{C}_{kl}\,d_{M}},\quad d_{M}=s_{k}-s_{l}-T_{M}, (147)

where C~k​l=Ck​l⊗I3\tilde{C}_{kl}=C_{kl}\otimes I_{3} with Ck​l=Ak​Ak​l−1​AlC_{kl}=A_{k}A_{kl}^{-1}A_{l} positive definite, and f⁡(dM)f(d_{M}) is an operator-specific function (a polynomial for kinetic energy, a screened Coulomb factor for potential energy, etc.).

Convergence of (147) is governed by the smallest eigenvalue cminc_{\min} of Ck​lC_{kl}: the number of image shells needed scales as

Nshells∼(χcutcmin)3​n,N_{\mathrm{shells}}\sim\left(\frac{\chi_{\mathrm{cut}}}{\sqrt{c_{\min}}}\right)^{3n}, (148)

where χcut2≈20\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{cut}}\approx 20–3030 is the truncation threshold for double precision. When basis functions are diffuse (AkA_{k} has small eigenvalues), Ck​lC_{kl} inherits small eigenvalues, cmin→0c_{\min}\to 0, and NshellsN_{\mathrm{shells}} diverges. This is the regime where the direct-space sum becomes prohibitively expensive and a dual representation is needed.

J.2 The diagonal case: Jacobi theta functions

J.2.1 Factorization of the sum

When Ck​lC_{kl} is diagonal, Ck​l=diag⁡(c1,…,cn)C_{kl}=\mathrm{diag}(c_{1},\dots,c_{n}), and the shift difference is dM=(sk,1−sl,1−m1​L,…)d_{M}=(s_{k,1}-s_{l,1}-m_{1}L,\dots), the image weight factorizes over the 3​n3n Cartesian directions α=1,…,3​n\alpha=1,\dots,3n:

∑M∈ℤ3​nωM=∏α=13​n∑mα∈ℤe−cα​(sk,α−sl,α−mα​Lα)2⏟=:ϑα.\sum_{M\in\mathbb{Z}^{3n}}\omega_{M}=\prod_{\alpha=1}^{3n}\underbrace{\sum_{m_{\alpha}\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-c_{\alpha}(s_{k,\alpha}-s_{l,\alpha}-m_{\alpha}L_{\alpha})^{2}}}_{\displaystyle=:\,\vartheta_{\alpha}}. (149)

Each factor ϑα\vartheta_{\alpha} is a Jacobi theta function. Recall the standard definition

ϑ3​(z|τ)=∑m∈ℤei​π​τ​m2+2​π​i​m​z.\vartheta_{3}(z\,|\,\tau)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{i\pi\tau m^{2}+2\pi imz}. (150)

Setting

τα=i​cα​Lα2π,zα=i​cα​(sk,α−sl,α)​Lαπ,\tau_{\alpha}=\frac{ic_{\alpha}L_{\alpha}^{2}}{\pi},\qquad z_{\alpha}=\frac{ic_{\alpha}(s_{k,\alpha}-s_{l,\alpha})L_{\alpha}}{\pi}, (151)

each factor in (149) equals ϑ3​(zα|τα)\vartheta_{3}(z_{\alpha}|\tau_{\alpha}) up to an overall exponential prefactor, so

∑M∈ℤ3​nωM=∏α=13​nϑ3​(zα|τα).\sum_{M\in\mathbb{Z}^{3n}}\omega_{M}=\prod_{\alpha=1}^{3n}\vartheta_{3}(z_{\alpha}\,|\,\tau_{\alpha}). (152)

J.2.2 The Jacobi imaginary transformation

The theta function satisfies the Jacobi imaginary transformation (Eq. J1 of the paper):

ϑ3(z|τ)=1−i​τe−iz2/(πτ)ϑ3(zτ|−1τ).\vartheta_{3}(z\,|\,\tau)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{-i\tau}}\,e^{-iz^{2}/(\pi\tau)}\,\vartheta_{3}\!\left(\frac{z}{\tau}\,\bigg|\,-\frac{1}{\tau}\right). (153)

This identity maps a theta function with modular parameter τ\tau to one with parameter −1/τ-1/\tau. The direct sum ϑ3​(z|τ)\vartheta_{3}(z|\tau) converges like e−π​|Im​τ|​m2e^{-\pi|\mathrm{Im}\,\tau|m^{2}}, while the dual sum ϑ3(z/τ|−1/τ)\vartheta_{3}(z/\tau|-1/\tau) converges like e−π|Im(−1/τ)|m2=e−πm2/|Imτ|e^{-\pi|\mathrm{Im}(-1/\tau)|m^{2}}=e^{-\pi m^{2}/|\mathrm{Im}\,\tau|}. Their convergence rates are therefore reciprocal.

J.2.3 Convergence analysis

Identifying Im​τα=cα​Lα2/π\mathrm{Im}\,\tau_{\alpha}=c_{\alpha}L_{\alpha}^{2}/\pi:

Regime cαc_{\alpha} Direct sum Dual sum
Diffuse basis small slow: e−cα​L2​m2e^{-c_{\alpha}L^{2}m^{2}} fast: e−π2m2/(cαL2)e^{-\pi^{2}m^{2}/(c_{\alpha}L^{2})}
Compact basis large fast: e−cα​L2​m2e^{-c_{\alpha}L^{2}m^{2}} slow: e−π2m2/(cαL2)e^{-\pi^{2}m^{2}/(c_{\alpha}L^{2})}

One always evaluates whichever representation converges faster. The crossover occurs when the two rates are equal, i.e. cα​Lα2=πc_{\alpha}L_{\alpha}^{2}=\pi, or equivalently cα=π/Lα\sqrt{c_{\alpha}}=\pi/L_{\alpha}.

J.3 The general case: Poisson summation formula

When Ck​lC_{kl} is not diagonal (the generic situation for correlated Gaussians with off-diagonal AkA_{k}), the sum (147) does not factorize. The multidimensional generalization of the Jacobi transformation is the Poisson summation formula applied to the Gaussian function g⁡(x)=e−x⊤​C~k​l​xg(x)=e^{-x^{\top}\tilde{C}_{kl}\,x}.

J.3.1 Result

∑M∈ℤ3​ne−dM⊤​C~k​l​dM=π3​n/2(detCk​l)3/2​Ωn∑K∈𝒢ne−K⊤(C~k​l)−1K/4ei​K⊤​(sk−sl),\sum_{M\in\mathbb{Z}^{3n}}e^{-d_{M}^{\top}\tilde{C}_{kl}\,d_{M}}=\frac{\pi^{3n/2}}{(\det C_{kl})^{3/2}\,\Omega^{n}}\sum_{K\in\mathcal{G}^{n}}e^{-K^{\top}(\tilde{C}_{kl})^{-1}K/4}\,e^{iK^{\top}(s_{k}-s_{l})}, (154)

where:

  • •

    𝒢n\mathcal{G}^{n} is the 3​n3n-dimensional reciprocal lattice with vectors

    K=2​π​(k1,xLx,k1,yLy,k1,zLz,…,kn,xLx,kn,yLy,kn,zLz),ki,μ∈ℤ;K=2\pi\!\left(\frac{k_{1,x}}{L_{x}},\frac{k_{1,y}}{L_{y}},\frac{k_{1,z}}{L_{z}},\dots,\frac{k_{n,x}}{L_{x}},\frac{k_{n,y}}{L_{y}},\frac{k_{n,z}}{L_{z}}\right),\quad k_{i,\mu}\in\mathbb{Z};
  • •

    Ωn=(Lx​Ly​Lz)n\Omega^{n}=(L_{x}L_{y}L_{z})^{n} is the nn-electron cell volume;

  • •

    detCk​l\det C_{kl} enters via the standard Gaussian Fourier transform identity ∫ℝNe−x⊤​C​x​𝑑x=πN/2/(detC)1/2\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}e^{-x^{\top}Cx}\,dx=\pi^{N/2}/(\det C)^{1/2}.

J.3.2 Derivation sketch

The Poisson summation formula states that for any sufficiently regular function g:ℝN→ℂg:\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{C} and lattice Λ⊂ℝN\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} with dual lattice Λ∗\Lambda^{*}:

∑v∈Λg⁡(x+v)=1vol⁡(Λ)​∑K∈Λ∗g^​(K)​ei​K⋅x,\sum_{v\in\Lambda}g(x+v)=\frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(\Lambda)}\sum_{K\in\Lambda^{*}}\hat{g}(K)\,e^{iK\cdot x}, (155)

where g^(K)=∫ℝNg(y)e−iK⋅ydy\hat{g}(K)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}g(y)\,e^{-iK\cdot y}\,dy is the Fourier transform. Applying this with g⁡(y)=e−y⊤​C~k​l​yg(y)=e^{-y^{\top}\tilde{C}_{kl}y}, Λ={TM:M∈ℤ3​n}\Lambda=\{T_{M}:M\in\mathbb{Z}^{3n}\}, x=sk−slx=s_{k}-s_{l}, and using

g^(K)=∫ℝ3​ne−y⊤​C~k​l​y−i​K⋅ydy=π3​n/2(detCk​l)3/2e−K⊤(C~k​l)−1K/4\hat{g}(K)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3n}}e^{-y^{\top}\tilde{C}_{kl}y-iK\cdot y}\,dy=\frac{\pi^{3n/2}}{(\det C_{kl})^{3/2}}\,e^{-K^{\top}(\tilde{C}_{kl})^{-1}K/4} (156)

yields (154) directly.

J.4 Convergence of the dual sum and optimal switching

J.4.1 Convergence rates

Let cminc_{\min} and cmax−1c_{\max}^{-1} denote the smallest eigenvalue of Ck​lC_{kl} and the largest eigenvalue of Ck​l−1C_{kl}^{-1} respectively. The number of significant terms in each representation is:

Ndirect∼(χcutcmin)3​n,Ndual∼(2​χcut​cmax2​π/L)3​n,N_{\mathrm{direct}}\sim\left(\frac{\chi_{\mathrm{cut}}}{\sqrt{c_{\min}}}\right)^{3n},\qquad N_{\mathrm{dual}}\sim\left(\frac{2\chi_{\mathrm{cut}}\sqrt{c_{\max}}}{2\pi/L}\right)^{3n}, (157)

where LL is a representative cell dimension and χcut2≈20\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{cut}}\approx 20–3030. The product Ndirect⋅NdualN_{\mathrm{direct}}\cdot N_{\mathrm{dual}} is independent of cminc_{\min}, confirming the reciprocal nature of the two representations.

J.4.2 Optimal switching criterion

Equating Ndirect=NdualN_{\mathrm{direct}}=N_{\mathrm{dual}} gives the crossover condition:

cmin​cmax≈π2L2.c_{\min}\,c_{\max}\approx\frac{\pi^{2}}{L^{2}}. (158)

In practice one evaluates

Use direct sum if ​cmin≳πL2,use dual sum otherwise.\text{Use direct sum if }c_{\min}\gtrsim\frac{\pi}{L^{2}},\quad\text{use dual sum otherwise.} (159)

J.5 Connection to the Ewald method

The Poisson summation approach for the image sum is the exact analogue of Ewald summation for the Coulomb lattice sum. Table 5 summarizes the parallel.

The key advantage of the Poisson route for Gaussian basis sets is that the Fourier transform of a Gaussian is again a Gaussian — no auxiliary splitting parameter κ\kappa or tt-integration is required. The dual sum (154) is therefore algebraically simpler than the Ewald decomposition, at the cost of requiring Ck​lC_{kl} to be invertible (which is always guaranteed by positive definiteness).

Appendix K Connection to Pair-Correlation–Single-Particle Gaussian Bases

K.1 The alternative basis form

A second class of many-electron Gaussian basis functions appearing in the literature takes the form

ψ(𝐫)=exp[−12∑i,j=1nAi​j𝐫i⋅𝐫j−∑i=1nβi|𝐫i−𝐬i|2],\psi(\mathbf{r})=\exp\!\left[-\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}A_{ij}\,\mathbf{r}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{j}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\beta_{i}\,|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{s}_{i}|^{2}\right], (160)

where A=(Ai​j)∈ℝn×nA=(A_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is a symmetric matrix of pair-coupling constants (not necessarily positive definite), each βi>0\beta_{i}>0 is a single-particle Gaussian width, and 𝐬i∈ℝ3\mathbf{s}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} is the center of the ii-th single-particle factor. The first sum encodes inter-electronic correlations through the unshifted quadratic 𝐫i⋅𝐫j\mathbf{r}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{j}; the second sum is a product of Gaussians each centered at 𝐬i\mathbf{s}_{i}.

We show that Eq. (160) is a special case of the SCG basis Eq. (11) and derive the exact correspondence between the two parameter sets.

K.2 Reduction to standard quadratic form

Expand the single-particle terms: βi​|𝐫i−𝐬i|2=βi​|𝐫i|2−2​βi​𝐫i⋅𝐬i+βi​|𝐬i|2\beta_{i}|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{s}_{i}|^{2}=\beta_{i}|\mathbf{r}_{i}|^{2}-2\beta_{i}\mathbf{r}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{s}_{i}+\beta_{i}|\mathbf{s}_{i}|^{2}. Absorbing the constant ∑iβi​|𝐬i|2\sum_{i}\beta_{i}|\mathbf{s}_{i}|^{2} into an overall normalization, the exponent of ψ\psi becomes

−12∑i,jAi​j𝐫i⋅𝐫j−∑iβi|𝐫i|2+2∑iβi𝐫i⋅𝐬i.-\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\,\mathbf{r}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{j}-\sum_{i}\beta_{i}|\mathbf{r}_{i}|^{2}+2\sum_{i}\beta_{i}\,\mathbf{r}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{s}_{i}. (161)

Combining the quadratic parts and introducing the diagonal matrix Dβ=diag⁡(β1,…,βn)D_{\beta}=\mathrm{diag}(\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{n}):

−12∑i,j(Ai​j+2βiδi​j)𝐫i⋅𝐫j+∑i 2βi𝐫i⋅𝐬i.-\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j}(A_{ij}+2\beta_{i}\delta_{ij})\,\mathbf{r}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{j}+\sum_{i}\,2\beta_{i}\,\mathbf{r}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{s}_{i}. (162)

Define the effective matrix

B≡12​(A+2​Dβ)∈ℝn×n.B\equiv\tfrac{1}{2}(A+2D_{\beta})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. (163)

Positive definiteness of BB (required for normalizability) demands that A+2​Dβ≻0A+2D_{\beta}\succ 0; equivalently, all eigenvalues of AA must exceed −2​mini​βi-2\min_{i}\beta_{i}. The exponent (162) is then

−𝐫T​(B⊗I3)​𝐫+2​(Dβ⊗I3)​𝐬⋅𝐫,-\mathbf{r}^{T}(B\otimes I_{3})\mathbf{r}+2\bigl(D_{\beta}\otimes I_{3}\bigr)\mathbf{s}\cdot\mathbf{r}, (164)

where 𝐬=(𝐬1,…,𝐬n)T∈ℝ3​n\mathbf{s}=(\mathbf{s}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{s}_{n})^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{3n}. Completing the square about the center

𝐫¯=(B⊗I3)−1​(Dβ⊗I3)​𝐬=(B−1​Dβ⊗I3)​𝐬,\bar{\mathbf{r}}=(B\otimes I_{3})^{-1}(D_{\beta}\otimes I_{3})\,\mathbf{s}=(B^{-1}D_{\beta}\otimes I_{3})\,\mathbf{s}, (165)

the exponent becomes

−(𝐫−𝐫¯)T​(B⊗I3)​(𝐫−𝐫¯)+𝐫¯T​(B⊗I3)​𝐫¯.-(\mathbf{r}-\bar{\mathbf{r}})^{T}(B\otimes I_{3})(\mathbf{r}-\bar{\mathbf{r}})+\bar{\mathbf{r}}^{T}(B\otimes I_{3})\bar{\mathbf{r}}. (166)

Hence, up to the constant e𝐫¯T​(B⊗I3)​𝐫¯−∑iβi​|𝐬i|2e^{\bar{\mathbf{r}}^{T}(B\otimes I_{3})\bar{\mathbf{r}}-\sum_{i}\beta_{i}|\mathbf{s}_{i}|^{2}} (which is absorbed into the variational coefficient),

ψ⁡(𝐫)∝exp⁡[−(𝐫−𝐫¯)T​(B⊗I3)​(𝐫−𝐫¯)].\psi(\mathbf{r})\propto\exp\!\bigl[-(\mathbf{r}-\bar{\mathbf{r}})^{T}(B\otimes I_{3})(\mathbf{r}-\bar{\mathbf{r}})\bigr]. (167)

This is precisely the SCG form (11) with identification

Ak=B=12(A+2Dβ),𝐬k=𝐫¯=(B−1Dβ⊗I3)𝐬.\boxed{A_{k}=B=\tfrac{1}{2}(A+2D_{\beta}),\qquad\mathbf{s}_{k}=\bar{\mathbf{r}}=(B^{-1}D_{\beta}\otimes I_{3})\,\mathbf{s}.} (168)

K.3 Inverse map: SCG parameters to the alternative form

Given an SCG with parameters (Ak,𝐬k)(A_{k},\mathbf{s}_{k}), the alternative-form parameters (A,Dβ,𝐬)(A,D_{\beta},\mathbf{s}) satisfying Eq. (168) are not unique: DβD_{\beta} is a free positive-definite diagonal matrix subject only to A=2​Ak−2​DβA=2A_{k}-2D_{\beta} being the desired pair-coupling matrix (which may have any sign on its diagonal). Choosing DβD_{\beta} fixes everything:

A=2​(Ak−Dβ),𝐬i=1βi​∑j=1n(Ak)i​j​𝐬k,j.A=2(A_{k}-D_{\beta}),\qquad\mathbf{s}_{i}=\frac{1}{\beta_{i}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(A_{k})_{ij}\,\mathbf{s}_{k,j}. (169)

Here 𝐬k,j∈ℝ3\mathbf{s}_{k,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} is the 3D block of 𝐬k\mathbf{s}_{k} corresponding to electron jj. The second relation follows from Dβ​𝐬=Ak​𝐬kD_{\beta}\mathbf{s}=A_{k}\mathbf{s}_{k} (i.e. B​𝐫¯=Dβ​𝐬B\bar{\mathbf{r}}=D_{\beta}\mathbf{s} with 𝐫¯=𝐬k\bar{\mathbf{r}}=\mathbf{s}_{k}).

Three natural choices of DβD_{\beta} are physically illuminating.

Choice 1: Dβ=diag⁡(Ak)D_{\beta}=\mathrm{diag}(A_{k}).

The diagonal of AkA_{k} is absorbed entirely into the single-particle widths, βi=(Ak)i​i\beta_{i}=(A_{k})_{ii}, and the pair-coupling matrix becomes Ai​j=2​(Ak)i​j​(1−δi​j)A_{ij}=2(A_{k})_{ij}(1-\delta_{ij}) — purely off-diagonal. This is the most natural separation of single-particle and correlation content. The single-particle centers are

𝐬i=1(Ak)i​i​∑j(Ak)i​j​𝐬k,j.\mathbf{s}_{i}=\frac{1}{(A_{k})_{ii}}\sum_{j}(A_{k})_{ij}\,\mathbf{s}_{k,j}. (170)
Choice 2: Dβ=AkD_{\beta}=A_{k}.

Here A=0A=0 (no explicit pair coupling) and βi=(Ak)i​i\beta_{i}=(A_{k})_{ii}… but this requires AkA_{k} to be diagonal for self-consistency (since A=2​Ak−2​Ak=0A=2A_{k}-2A_{k}=0 regardless, while 𝐬i=𝐬k,i\mathbf{s}_{i}=\mathbf{s}_{k,i}). More precisely, this choice sets 𝐬i=(Ak)i​i−1​∑j(Ak)i​j​𝐬k,j\mathbf{s}_{i}=(A_{k})_{ii}^{-1}\sum_{j}(A_{k})_{ij}\mathbf{s}_{k,j}, which reduces to 𝐬i=𝐬k,i\mathbf{s}_{i}=\mathbf{s}_{k,i} only if AkA_{k} is diagonal. When AkA_{k} is diagonal the two bases are identical, recovering independent-particle Gaussians ∏ie−βi​|𝐫i−𝐬i|2\prod_{i}e^{-\beta_{i}|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{s}_{i}|^{2}}.

Choice 3: Equal widths βi=β\beta_{i}=\beta (all electrons same width).

This is the simplest variational ansatz; with Dβ=β​ID_{\beta}=\beta I and A=2​(Ak−β​I)A=2(A_{k}-\beta I):

𝐬i=1β​∑j(Ak)i​j​𝐬k,j.\mathbf{s}_{i}=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{j}(A_{k})_{ij}\,\mathbf{s}_{k,j}. (171)
